title: 1.e4 Part 3: Caro etc
description: In Part 3 of the e4 course, we address the Caro-Kann, French, Pirc, Modern, Philidor, Scandinavian, and other random defenses.

2k2bnr/ppprqppp/2n1p3/1N2N2b/3P1B2/7P/P1.text:
And we're recapturing the pawn with a winning position. 

Black is uncoordinated and we're going to win some material, with an attack on the king.

Everything is loose in the Black camp.

2k4r/ppp3p1/2nb1q1n/4p3/5pp1/2PP2P1/PP2B.text:
The good thing about being up material is that you can give some back and still have a winning position and more material. 

We are ready to face ...f3 here and sacrifice.

White is winning.

2k4r/ppp3p1/2nb1q1n/4pp2/6p1/1QPP2P1/PP2.text:
The rook captures our knight.

But we are solid.

2kr1b1N/ppp3p1/2n2q1n/4pp2/6p1/1QP5/PP1P.text:
Black tries preventing the escape of the knight.

But with d3 we attack the knight and pose even more problems.

2kr1b1r/ppp1ppp1/2n2n2/3q3p/6b1/2P2N1P/P.text:
Not placing any pawns in the center isn't ideal.

We do put a pawn in the center, though. 

Black's position isn't bad yet, but it can become so if they don't play actively.

2kr1b1r/ppp2p2/2n1pn2/3q2pp/3P2b1/2P2N1P.text:
One of Black's potential plans is always a kingside attack.

But we are unbothered: development and a solid position allow us to defend any incoming unsound attacks.

2kr1b1r/ppp2p2/2n1pn2/3q2pp/3P4/2P2b1P/P.text:
In order for the attack to progress Black has to take.

But we recapture, with a strong bishop.

2kr1b1r/ppp2p2/2q1pn2/6pp/3P4/2P2Q1P/PP1.text:
We attack the queen and the knight. 

This represents a better endgame for us. 

Black's g5- and h5-pawns are weak.

2kr1b1r/ppp2p2/2q1pn2/6pp/3P4/2P4P/PP1N1.text: After we attract the queen to c6 we have a simplification tactic.

2kr1b1r/ppp2pp1/2n1pn2/3q3p/3P2b1/2P2N1P.text:
This passive continuation is the most common.

I like Re1 because we improve our rook, but we also get access to f1.

Our king won't get mated easily.

2kr1b1r/pppq1p2/2n1pn2/6pp/3P4/2P2B1P/PP.text:
The queen retreats to d7. 

At this point, I like simplifying. 

Sometimes, there's a clear way to end an attack and we have to take it.

First we'll capture.

2kr1b1r/pppq1ppp/2n1pn2/8/8/2P2B1P/PP1P1.text:
Black develops their knight to f6.

And we get the strong d4-pawn in the center. 

The e5-square is completely under our control.

2kr1bnr/ppp1ppp1/2n5/3q3p/6b1/5N1P/PPPPB.text:
The move ...h5 is yet another fishing hook idea where Black hopes to open the h-file and create a strong attack.

Our plan is to play d4, not to take the bishop and play Black's game. 

We want to first prepare it with c3.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n1q3/4N3/8/2N4P/P1PPQP.text:
Another example that we can see is if the knight comes back to c6.

We can give it up entirely for the attack on the b-file!

That's how potent our b4 and b5 idea is.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q3b/8/5N1P/PPPPBPP.text:
Black slides the bishop back to h5.

We finally develop the queenside knight with tempo on Black's queen.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBPP.text:
Black castles their king.

Let's ask the bishop a question now.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/8/5b1P/PPPPBPP1.text:
The capture on f3 is quite natural. 

We like to see it because we get the bishop pair.

We recapture, with a powerful bishop aiming at the light squares towards the king.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/7b/1q6/2N2N1P/P1PPB.text:
This move willingly puts the queen on the open file where it will be attacked.

We are now enjoying b-file compensation.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/q6b/8/2N2N1P/P1PPBP.text: If the queen goes back to a5, we can make use of the b-file.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/q6b/8/2N2N1P/PPPPBP.text:
Black moves the queen over to a5.

I had once recommended 8.a3 here, but 8.b4 is even stronger.

The idea is to sacrifice the b-pawn and open up the b-file since Black has committed to the queenside.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/qR5b/8/2N2N1P/P1PPB.text: We're cashing in with this double attack.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/2nq4/7b/8/2N2N1P/P1PPBP.text:
The queen has to go to safety.

Before we move our pieces further, it's principled to control the center.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/1Q2n3/8/2N4P/P1PP1P.text:
The knight takes on e5. 

You'd think Black is safe because b7 is only one pawn.

The problem is the king isn't safe and the rook cannot defend by itself. 

Black's kingside is also out of the game.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/4N3/1n6/2N4P/P1PPQP.text:
Black moves the queen to e6.

We continue with Rb1, attacking Black's knight and placing the rook on the semi-open b-file.

White now has a very comfortable advantage and great attacking prospects on the queenside.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/4N3/4Q3/2N4P/P1nP1P.text:
We have a double attack. 

After something like ...c6 there's the crazy Nb5. 

Black's king isn't safe and they're losing because of it.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/4q3/4N3/8/2N4P/P1nPQPP1.text:
The ambitious ...Nxc2 wins a pawn but doesn't work.

We're winning.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/7R/8/5N1P/2PPBPP1/2Bn.text:
And the knight is trapped on d1. 

We will go up material.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/q6b/1n6/2N2N1P/P1PPBP.text:
Having the knight capture on b4 is the most natural. 

That way, Rb1 doesn't come with a tempo.

We get our rook on the b-file anyway.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/q6b/8/2N2N1P/n1PPBPP1.text:
This continuation is very greedy.

Our double attack works.

2kr1bnr/ppp1pppp/8/qR5b/8/2n2N1P/2PPBPP1.text:
This capture comes with an attack on the queen.

But we're attacking the bishop too!

2kr1bnr/ppp1qppp/2n1p3/1N5b/3P4/5N1P/P1P.text:
The queen moves away.

We develop our bishop with a tempo.

Now the c7-pawn is under fire.

2kr1bnr/ppp2Np1/2n2q2/4pp2/6p1/1QP5/PP1P.text:
The queen goes to f6.

We take on h8.

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/2n5/3qp2p/6b1/2P2N1P/PP1.text:
Black plays e5 to control the center, which is one of their best approaches.

When there's a fishing hook trap like this with a pawn on the 5th rank, Black will take longer to reach the h-file since the e5-pawn blocks the queen.

Hence, we can capture.

2kr1bnr/ppp2pp1/2n5/3qp3/6p1/2P2N2/PP1PB.text:
Black recaptures and the h-file is opened.

But we put yet another piece on the 5th rank, slowing down Black's counterplay.

The g4-pawn is also under attack now.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2nqp3/7b/3P4/2N2N1P/P1P1.text:
Black pushes a pawn and tries to catch up on development.

But we're too quick with the attack!

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2q1p3/7b/2P5/P4N1P/3PBPP.text: The queen goes to the c6-square.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/2q1p3/7b/2PP4/P4N1P/4BPP.text:
But our attack plays itself.

Black won't have the answer to the upcoming aggression.

We are looking to play d5 and place our queen and the bishop on b3 and e3.

We will attack on the b-file and down the diagonal.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3q3b/8/P4N1P/2PPBPP1.text:
The queen recaptures.

But all our moves come with tempi.

The c-pawn advances first to grab more central space.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/q2n3b/8/P1N2N1P/2PPB.text:
The knight goes to d5 where it hopes to obstruct the efficacy of our Rb5 move.

We'll take.

2kr1bnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/q6b/1n6/2N2N1P/P1PPB.text:
The move ...e6 lends some support to the knight.

It's time for us to make use of our b-file pressure.

So, we'll attack the knight.

2kr1bnr/ppp3p1/2n5/3qppN1/6p1/2P5/PP1PBP.text:
Black defends g4.

Not only is Qb3 a queen trade proposal, it's our pieces converging on f7.

2kr1bnr/ppp3p1/2nq4/4ppN1/6p1/1QP5/PP1PB.text:
Black avoids the trade, which allows us to jump to f7.

This is a family fork.

2kr1bnr/pppq1ppp/2n1p3/1P6/8/2N2b1P/P1PP.text:
Black captures on f3. 

This move gives up the bishop pair but frees up the d4-square for the knight.

We recapture on f3 with the bishop.

2kr1bnr/pppq1ppp/2n1p3/7b/1P6/2N2N1P/P1P.text:
Black doesn't capture the pawn, and instead continues with ...e6.

We push our b-pawn up to b5 and attack Black's knight!

That's our main idea if Black doesn't accept the b4-pawn.

2kr1bnr/pppq1ppp/2n1p3/8/8/5B1P/PPPP1PP1.text:
Black's plan is easy in this equal position, as they want to develop the pieces to d6 and f6. 

We're going to develop our pieces as well, but we also want to make sure we have a strong center. 

The move c3 serves to prepare d4.

2kr1bnr/pppq1ppp/4p3/1P6/3n4/2N2B1P/P1PP.text:
And we support the b5-pawn with Rb1. 

White now has an objective edge and great attacking prospects on the queenside, and we'll look to continue with d3, a4 and Be3. 

A model game from this position is Ponomariov - Fressinet, 2016.

Here's the link to that game:
https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1816890
Black jumps the knight into d4.

2kr1bnr/pppqpppp/2n5/7b/8/2N2N1P/PPPPBPP.text:
Black retreats the queen back to d7.

We'll play the stunning b4!

Let's see what Black wants to do.

2kr1bnr/pppqpppp/2n5/8/8/5B1P/PPPP1PP1/R.text:
The queen retreats, keeping an eye on the c6-knight.

We centralize the rook.

Another natural improving move.

2kr1bnr/pppqpppp/8/4N3/1n6/2N4P/P1PPbPP1.text:
Black captures the bishop on e2.

We recapture with the queen.

2kr1bnr/pppqpppp/8/7b/1n6/2N2N1P/P1PPBPP.text:
Black captures the pawn, but this is simply too dangerous!

We jump our knight into e5, attacking Black's queen and opening up a discovered attack on Black's bishop!

2kr3N/ppp3p1/2nb1q1n/4pp2/6p1/1QPP4/PP2B.text:
Black wants to take the knight, and we can't really defend or move it.

But we can use this time to solidify and slow the pawns and pieces marching forward. 

g2 is also a great square for our king since we control the light squares.

2kr3r/ppp2pp1/2nb1nq1/5p1p/3P3N/2PB4/PP3.text:
And once again as we see many times in this chapter, the queen is trapped.

Well done!

2kr3r/ppp2pp1/2nbpn2/3q3p/3P2b1/2P2N1P/P.text:
Black may develop their bishop to d6.

The knight has many options. 

The f1-square allows our pieces to pivot and defend our king.

2kr3r/ppp2pp1/2nbpn2/5q1p/3P2b1/2P2N1P/P.text:
Black has a clear plan. 

But we have enough pieces to thwart this attack.

We transport our knight to defend the king.

2kr3r/ppp2pp1/2nbpn2/5q1p/3P4/2P2N1b/PP2.text:
Black takes, but they aren't winning, nor do they have a forced draw.

We first attack the queen.

2kr3r/ppp2pp1/2nbpnq1/5b1p/3P4/2PBNN2/PP.text:
This move seems normal but it's a mistake.

We capture on f5.

2kr3r/ppp2pp1/2nbpnq1/7p/3P4/2P1NN1b/PP2.text:
The queen pins our pawn.

But we have a bishop that we can use to harass the queen. 

There are simply too many defenders.

2kr3r/pppq1ppp/2nbpn2/8/3P4/2P2B1P/PP1N1.text:
But we are going to attack the bishop to remove it from d6. 

If Black allows it, their position can become passive very quickly as you can see here. 

White is better.

2kr3r/pppq1ppp/2nbpn2/8/3P4/2P2B1P/PP3PP.text: The bishop goes to d6, aiming at the kingside but most importantly that central e5-square.

3r1bnr/pQpkpppp/3q2n1/3P4/4N3/7P/P1P2PP1.text:
We attack it, and force it away. 

This allows us to continue attacking the king and White is winning. 

All of this from our b4-idea!

3r1bnr/pQpkpppp/3q2n1/3P4/8/2N4P/P1P2PP1.text: The queen is the only defender, but it's easy to attack.

3r1bnr/pQpkpppp/4q1n1/8/3P4/2N4P/P1P2PP1.text:
The knight goes to g6.

And we attack the queen, pushing with tempo.

3r1bnr/pQpkpppp/4q3/4n3/8/2N4P/P1PP1PP1/.text:
The king goes to d7. 

Without more material joining the attack, White wouldn't be doing well.

But we've got the pawn!

r3kbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPPBPPP.text:
In this setup, it's clear that Black is about to castle queenside, so there is no point in us going d4 to give them a target on the d-file. 

We'll just castle our king and go from there.

rn2kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/6b1/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black develops the light-squared bishop to g4 and pins our knight 22% of the time.

We'll support and unpin the knight by developing our bishop to e2.

rnb1kbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3q4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RNB.text:
Black recaptures with the queen 72% of the time.

Against the Scandinavian, I'm going to recommend the flexible Nf3 system, where we hope to develop with Be2, O-O, d4/c4 and so on. 

The Scandi has various setups for Black and general ideas to follow,  but overall White's ideas are the same.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
11% of the time, Black replies with 1...d5, The Scandivanian Defense,  and it was played in more than 400 million games.

The main idea behind 1...d5 is to trade off the central pawns and get the queen out early so that Black can develop the queenside quickly, often choosing to castle long.

We'll take the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Since it's an increasingly popular opening for Black, let's learn how to deal with the Scandinavian. 

In this study we'll see what to do after Black's most popular move: 2...Qxd5.

2kr1b1r/B1pqnppp/1p3n2/3Pp3/2P5/5B2/PP3P.text:
Black tries to trap our bishop, but we were ready for this.

We'll develop the knight.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/3q4/3P2b1/5N2/PPP.text:
Black castles their king and threatens to capture the d4-pawn.

That's why we will support the d-pawn by developing our dark-squared bishop to e3. 

Keep in mind that once Black lines up on the d-file and targets our d4-pawn, we have to consider ...e5 as an option at all times.

2kr1b1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/5q2/3P2b1/4BN2/PP.text:
This move applies more pressure on the knight, but it also makes the rook more effective on the d-file.

Bringing out our other knight to d2 helps us block the d-file and overprotect our knight.

2kr1b1r/ppp2pp1/5n1p/q2Pn1N1/2PBp3/8/PP2.text:
Black counterattacks our knight.

But we can win the pawn on e4.

2kr1b1r/ppp2pp1/7p/q2PB3/2P1n3/8/PP2QPPP.text:
Black is in a lot of trouble. They are down material and we control the center. 

This should be easy to convert.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3q3b/3P4/4BN1P/PP.text:
There's a chance Black won't play ...h5 but rather move the bishop to the h5-square.

After the bishop goes to h5, I like attacking the queen because it has less options on the 5th rank.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3q4/3P2b1/4BN2/PP.text:
Black continues with ...e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop.

We should play h3 to attack the bishop and entice Black to move to the h-file.

It's very important that if 8...h5 you remember the simple 9.Nbd2 and simply develop.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/5q1b/2PP4/4BN1P/P.text:
If the queen goes to f5, this is a much more aggressive position for the queen. 

We'll develop our knight to c3.

All normal thus far.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3qp3/3P2b1/4BN2/PP.text:
Black does strike in the center with ...e5.

We'll grab a tempo on the queen with c4.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4Nq2/3P4/4B3/PPPNb.text:
This initiates some trades.

We recapture. 

Our queen is on the e-file now, so Black's ...e5 push lacks utility.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2PPq1b1/4BN2/P.text:
If the queen moves up, it still exerts pressure on d4. 

The rook is also on the d-file, x-raying our queen.

That's why we should develop our knight, attacking the queen.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4pq2/2PP2b1/4BN2/P.text:
This is the queen's other option, but it doesn't change much.

First, we make sure the d-file remains closed a bit longer by pushing the pawn.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/4pq2/3P2b1/4BN2/PP.text:
The ...e5 break is always critical for Black. 

But as things stand, we're equipped to deal with it safely.

We'll take on e5.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q2P2N1/2P1p3/4B3/P.text:
Black takes, trying to win time.

We recapture. 

Now our d-pawn isn't pinned anymore and we are attacking both the knight and the f7-pawn.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q2P4/2P1p1b1/4BN2/.text:
Black might try to push ...e4 and attack our knight, since our d-pawn is pinned.

But we can simply jump to g5, attack the f7-pawn and offer a trade of bishops.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q2Pp3/2P3b1/4BN2/P.text:
We'll push the d-pawn up to d5. 

This shuts down the d-file pressure and keeps our position safer.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/q3p3/2PP2b1/4BN2/P.text:
Black moves the queen over to a5.

This signals that they don't want to commit to attacking the kingside.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2nq1/3P4/2P1p2N/4B3/PP.text:
I wouldn't be surprised if you find yourself winning a queen by simply being solid and developing your pieces, as it's trapped here.

Queens wandering off in the opening are a bad idea for beginners and intermediates.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2nq1/3P4/2P1p3/4BN2/PP.text: You may actually see this a lot in the Scandinavian: since the queen wanders off, it often runs out of squares.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2nq1/3Pp3/2P5/4Bb2/PP1.text:
The bishop takes on f3.

We'll recapture with the knight.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/2n2nq1/4p3/2PP2b1/4BN2/P.text:
The queen goes to g6. 

Black has pressure on d4, so we have to deal with it.

The best way to do this is by pushing the pawn and attacking the knight.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Ppq2/1nP3b1/4BN1P/P.text:
And now we can attack the bishop on g4. 

...Bxh3 doesn't work because we control over the center and we have enough pieces to defend the kingside.

Black's attempts have failed and we are much more active and developed with a borderline winning advantage.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Ppq2/1nP3b1/4BN2/PP.text: If Black wants to continue in aggressive fashion, they will jump to b4, looking at the c2-square.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4nq2/3P4/4B3/PPPNQPP.text:
Black trades on e5.

But this shouldn't be a problem at all.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4q3/8/4BN2/PPP1QPPP/.text:
And we improve our knight. 

...Qxb2 is simply bad for Black as Rab1 activates a rook on the b-file.

We want to improve our position with moves like Re1 and Bd4 when ready.

2kr1b1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/q2Pn1N1/2P1p3/4B3/PP.text:
Black centralizes, defending f7.

But we are persistent in attacking the defender of the f7-pawn.

Also, now both our knight and the queen attack the e4-pawn.

2kr1b1r/pppq1p2/2n1pn1p/6pb/2PP4/P3BN1P/.text:
Black may try to attack your kingside here.

But without fear, we continue on the queenside!

This expansion with b4 is crucial.

2kr1b1r/pppq1p2/2n1pn1p/7b/1PPP2p1/P3BN1.text:
Black attacks the knight and the h3-hook.

Jumping to e5 is fine here and allowing Black to take on h3 if they want to.

2kr1b1r/pppq1p2/4pn1p/4P2B/1PP5/P3B3/3N1.text: This desperado won't amount to anything.

Obviously we cannot take the pawn because we'd be exposed on the g-file.

We're up material and should win easily.

2kr1b1r/pppq1p2/4pn1p/4P2b/1PP5/P3B2p/3N.text:
This capture won't do Black any good, as they are sacrificing the bishop.

They'll lose material without a real attack.

We can take the bishop.

2kr1b1r/pppq1p2/4pn1p/4n2b/1PPP2p1/P3B2P.text:
Black trades the knights first.

We'll recapture, without being afraid of any d-file pressure.

2kr1b1r/pppq1pp1/2n1pn1p/7b/2PP4/4BN1P/P.text:
Black covers their g5-square, but also creates a square for the bishop.

We'll start focusing on the queenside, which is where our attacking prospects lie.

The move a3 prepares b4.

2kr1b1r/pppq1ppp/2n1pn2/7b/2PP4/4BN1P/PP.text:
If ...Qd7, the queen lacks much activity. 

It looks like the safest square, so that's why people may play it.

We can simply continue development.

2kr1b1r/pppq1ppp/2n2n2/3Pp3/2P5/4Bb2/PP2.text:
Black can throw in this capture on f3.

We'll simply recapture, keeping the bishop pair.

Black still has to move away.

2kr1b1r/pppq1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2PP2b1/4BN2/P.text:
Black can choose to go back to d7.

In that case, d5 is a logical move to avoid confrontation in the center and attack the knight.

2kr1b1r/pppqnppp/5n2/3Pp3/2P5/4BB2/PP3PP.text:
Once they do, the a7-pawn is undefended.

We'll take it.

2kr2r1/ppp2p1p/2B1pn2/2P2q2/QP1P4/2N1B1b.text:
Sure, Black can sacrifice.

We'll accept.

We'll recapture with the queen.

Our queen is active, and we've gotten rid of Black's developed bishop.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/3n4/3P2b1/5N2/PPP1B.text:
Black opens up the dark-squared bishop.

We'll castle. 

This is one of the benefits of our Nf3 variation: we get to castle quickly.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/3n4/3P4/3Q1N2/PPP2P.text:
This setup from Black isn't challenging at all. 

We'll even be able to kick the knight out of d5 with c4 at some point.

But first, we'll get our king to safety, enjoying control of e5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black doesn't recapture with the queen, and instead tries to avoid losing the lead in development by attacking the d5-pawn with the knight.

This happens almost 20% of the time and in more than 50 million games.

We'll pretty much ignore Black's move and continue with our standard plan involving Be2, O-O, and d4/c4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/8/3n4/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black captures the pawn on d5.

We should play d4 quickly if allowed.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/8/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.text:
This is called the Blackburne-Kloosterboer Gambit and it's played 4% of the time.

Black wants to gambit a pawn in order to accelerate their development.

This isn't the best choice if we know how to fight it. We'll accept.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
This study is for all the rest in the Scandinavian, 2...Nc6 and 2...b6. 

Here, basic opening principles apply and you can try to implement various ideas from other parts of the course.

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/1qn1p3/2bpP3/5B2/2NB1N2.text:
...Qb6 attacks both b2 and f2.

This is the most popular move.

We should defend the more important of the two pawns by castling and allow b2 to be taken!

We have a better position and we'll prove it.

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/5B2/2NB1N2/.text:
Black captures on b2 and attacks our knight.

But we'll jump to b5 and threaten a fork on c7.

It turns out that Black's queen has ventured too far from the rest of the Black pieces and can't defend.

r1b1k2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/8/Bb1NP3/5N2/P2P1P.text:
And White has pressure and better pieces than Black. 

Just to illustrate the pressure, the bishop on b4 is under attack because its defender is pinned.

If Black plays ...Bc5, Nxc6 is a tricky move to face. 

Because if Black recaptures with their knight, d4 for d5 is winning.

r1b1k2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/qB6/Qb1NP3/5N2/P2P.text:
Black defends again and offers a trade of queens.

I suggest we remain calm here and slide the rook to b1, attacking the bishop.

This basically forces Black to trade.

r1b2r2/pp1n1ppk/2n1p3/1NbpP3/5B2/5N2/PqP.text:
If the king takes, White is completely winning.

Check!

r1b2rk1/pp1n1pp1/2n1p3/1NbpP1N1/5B2/3Q4/.text:
And now, Qd3 so that Black doesn't play ...Qxc2.

There's no way to prevent infiltration at this point.

The evaluation is +4.2.

r1b2rk1/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/1NbpP3/5B2/3B1N2/.text:
If Black castles...

There's a Greek Gift.

r1bq1r2/pp1n1pp1/2n1p1k1/2bpP1N1/5B2/2N5.text:
And if the king refuses to go back...

Check on d3!

r1bq1r2/pp1n1ppk/2n1p3/2bpP3/5B2/2N2N2/P.text:
Just to demonstrate how a Greek Gift works, Black captures on h7.

It involves the knight coming to g5 with check first.

r1bq1r2/pp1n2p1/2n1p1k1/2bpPpN1/5B2/2N3Q.text:
And now we threaten all kinds of discovered attacks!

White is winning here since Black's king is too exposed.

r1bq1rk1/1p1nbppp/p1n1p3/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPN.text:
They develop their other knight.

The best square for our queen is e2.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/8/3P1B2/3B1N2/P.text:
And we develop our bishop, with an interesting game ahead that we'll play following the principles of IQP positions.

We will try to protect our d4-pawn as much as we can and turn it into an asset down the line.

On the other hand, Black will try to block it and leave it a liability for us.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPN.text: The knight comes to the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/5B2/2NB1N2.text:
Castling is also very popular, but never forget:

The Greek Gift sacrifice is an idea whenever you've got a pawn on e5, a knight on f3 and a bishop on d3.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1p3/2npP3/5B2/P1NB1N2.text:
And we'll castle as well. A common pawn break in these positions is ...f6 or ...f5. 

Against ...f6, we can play Re1 and recapture on e5 with the bishop. 

If Black plays ...f5, en passant and Bg3 are good ideas, with the Re1 idea always being a sound maneuver in these positions.

r1bqk1nr/pp2nppp/1b2p3/1P6/Q2pP3/5N2/PB1.text:
Bb2 exerts great pressure on the pawns and the diagonal. 

Black will most likely continue with ...Nf6, attacking e4. 

But their coordination isn't the best, so their piece pressure isn't good either.

If ...Nf6, Ng3 defends everything, and we're still prepared to play Nxd4.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/1bn1p3/8/QP1pP3/5N2/P2PN.text:
If the bishop goes back, we have a logical continuation.

I really like b5, attacking the knight.

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2b5/Q2pP3/5N2/PP1P.text:
...Bc5 is the most popular defense.

Black simply adds a defender to the pawn.

So how can we target that defender? With b4!

r1bqk1nr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/8/Qb1pP3/5N2/P2PNP.text:
The bishop takes.

We've successfully distracted the bishop and now we can win the pawn on d4.

This also pressures the knight on c6.

r1bqk2r/1p1n1ppp/p1n1p3/2bpP3/5B2/2NB1N2.text:
Black sometimes goes for ...a6, thinking of ...b5.

This is another approach they can take.

We'll just castle and let them play it.

r1bqk2r/3n1ppp/p1n1p3/1pbpP3/5B2/2NB1N2/.text:
We should overprotect e5.

White is doing well here.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2bpP3/8/2NB1N2/PP.text:
Black develops, attacking e5.

And we can develop, defending.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/2npP3/5B2/2NB1N2/P.text:
8...Be7 is the most natural continuation, clearing the way for castling.

And our setup consists of Bd3, a3 and O-O. 

With a3, we're preventing ...Nb4, and now the way is clear for O-O.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/2n1p3/8/Qb1NP3/5N2/P2P1P.text:
Black will get the kingside knight to e7 at some point to help with the defense of the pinned knight on c6.

In that case, it's best to develop with increasing pressure.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2n1p3/2PpP3/8/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black could delay capturing on c5, simply developing the knight. 

This is a sound approach, as it attacks the more important e5-pawn.

We should defend this pawn, since in many positions it is a strong asset in our kingside attacks.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2npP3/5B2/2N2N2/PP.text:
And now instead of a transposition with ...Bxc5, Black could take on c5 with the knight, controlling some squares in our camp.

But we should still put our bishop on d3, controlling the e4-square. 

We're not concerned about ...Nxd3.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2p5/3pP3/2P2N2/PP1.text:
...Nc6 is the most popular move.

Let's capture once.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/8/3pP3/5N2/PP1PNPP.text:
Black recaptures.

And now we can pin the knight, threatening to win the pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4pn2/8/3QP3/5N2/PP1P1PP.text: And after the knight is developed...

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/4pn2/8/3QP3/5N2/PP1PBPP.text:
It's time to consolidate being a pawn up.

We'll play standard moves like d3 and O-O, and we can activate our dark-squared bishop via Bd2-Bc3.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/2n1p3/8/Q2pP3/5N2/PP1PN.text:
The bishop can come to d7 and unpin.

However, that gives us a pawn as we can just take on d4.

After this the computer recommends ...Nge7 for Black, but the most common move is certainly ...Nxd4.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/4p3/1B6/Q2NP3/3n1N2/PP1.text:
Don't be afraid of this check.

We can chase the knight away.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/4p3/1B6/Q2NPn2/5N2/PP1P.text:
Your king will be safe enough and you'll be a pawn up.

Black will try to develop with moves like ...Nf6, so you can continue with moves like Bxd7+, to get pieces off the board, followed by g3.
And if Black checks you again...

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/4p3/4n3/Q2NP3/5N2/PP1P1.text:
This discovered attack is very popular.

But we can just develop and block the attack.

The point of this move is that we'll just trade Black's attackers.

r2qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/4p3/8/Q2nP3/5N2/PP1P1PP.text:
Our queen is under attack now.

So we will recapture with it.

rnbq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1p3/1B6/3P4/5N2/PPN2.text:
If Black forces us away from the diagonal...

There's no reason to trade on c6.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1p3/1B6/8/5N2/PPNP1PP.text:
Black castles now.

And we activate our isolated Queen's pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2bpP3/8/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
Black recaptures.

Our bishop is well placed on the b1-h7 diagonal when the pawn is on e5.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2n1p3/1B6/3N4/5N2/PP1P1P.text:
Black gets ready to castle too.

We'll rotate the knight back to c2 in order to leave some space for the d4-thrust.

That's how we will activate in the center of the board.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2p1P3/3p4/2P2N2/PP.text:
Black keeps the pressure on e5.

We'll take on d4 and it looks like we're winning a pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/2ppP3/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black plays ...c5, undermining our structure.

This is the key move they have to know.

I actually recommend capturing on c5 because we don't have time to defend the d4-pawn with another pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4p3/4P3/3p4/5N2/PP1PNP.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll take with the e-knight so that the f-knight still guards the e5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/1B6/3N4/5N2/PP1P1P.text:
This knight must block instead.

Now we can castle.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/4n3/3N4/5N2/PP1P1PPP.text:
But Black had this tactic in mind. 

The idea is that if Nxe5, Black has ...Qxd4.

We'll give a check instead of falling for it.

We are trying to prompt Black to place a piece on the d-file and block their own queen.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/3pP3/2P2N2/PP1P.text:
...Nf6 attacks the e4-pawn.

Black is trying to complicate matters even more.

Let's push and counterattack.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Black activates the knight just over 20% of the time.

In most positions like this, we will push the pawn to e5 to grab some more space and attack the knight.

This makes our position easier to play and forces Black to rely on flank pawn breaks like ...c5.

rnbqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4p3/3pP3/8/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
Black usually goes to d7.

I now prefer d4, connecting the pawns.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2p5/3pP3/5N2/PPPPNPP.text:
And by far the most popular continuation is ...c5, claiming that central space.

It's best to immediately challenge the structure.

The move ...d3 isn't possible because the pawn is too far advanced and it can't be defended after Nf4.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
And once Black goes for d5...

We bring our other knight out. 

This is our starting position with the two knights on f3 and c3.

In this study, we'll analyze the 3...Nf6 and 3...d4 responses.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black pushes ...d4 just over a quarter of the time.

This move, attacking the knight, is the second most popular move in the database.

I suggest we bring our knight back, putting pressure on d4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black goes for the French 10% of the time, which is still almost 380 million games in the database!

The pawn on e6 supports the d5-advancement, but blocks in the bishop on c8.

We'll simply develop our knight for now.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
One of the many Chessly Weapons against the French Defense is The Two Knights French. 

White develops both knights and adopts a solid setup.

Let's learn about it in Chapter 2.

r1b1k1nr/pp2bppp/1qn5/1Bp5/3pN3/5N2/PPPP.text: Black tries to get the queen in.

r1b1k1nr/pp2bppp/1qnN4/1Bp5/3p4/5N2/PPPP.text:
But doing so loses castling rights.

After ...Kf8 we can take the knight on c6, followed by Nc4 and d3 to develop the dark-squared bishop.

Black will have trouble with their kingside coordination because of their uncastled king.

r1b1k2r/ppp2pp1/2nbpq1p/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP1.text:
Black might go for ...Nc6, trying to attack our d4-pawn.

But c3 is a simple defense.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/2nbpq1p/8/3P3P/2PB1N2/PP.text:
But we can go for an attack instead! 

The move h4 begins the pawn storm.

We'll continue with Be3, O-O-O, and try to unleash even more forces against the kingside.

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/2nbpq1p/8/3P4/2PB1N2/PP2.text: Castling now is a bit different, since if Qe4, Black has ...Qf5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
White can continue with Qe2, Bf4 and c3.

Black has a problem piece: the bishop on c8. Luckily White won't have any problems to develop. A strong grip on the e5-square will prevent any ...e5 pushes.

r1bqk1nr/pp2bppp/2n5/1Bp5/3p4/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
This block is by far the most popular.

Ne4 now attacks the c5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2bppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/3P4/2N2N2/PP.text:
And now even the very popular ...Be7 is inaccurate.

Ne5 puts more pressure on c6.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2PP.text:
And both sides will calmly castle.

White can continue with Qe2, Bf4 and c3.

Black has a problem piece: the bishop on c8. 

Luckily, White won't have any problems to develop. A strong grip on the e5-square will prevent any ...e5 pushes.

r1bqkb1r/p1p2p1p/1pn1pp2/8/3P4/4BN2/PPP2.text:
Since the doubled pawns prevent the light-squared bishop's development, what you'll often see is Black going for ...b6 and ...Bb7. 

I suggest just going for natural development here. 

We want to castle long since the g-file is open.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/8/2N2N2/PPPP.text:
Black usually develops the knight.

We have room to strike in the center now.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2p1p/2n1pp2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
What you'll often see is Black developing to c6. 

Our bishop can come and overprotect d4.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black recaptures.

The d3-square is best for our bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/8/3PN3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Once the knight comes to f6, we don't really have a reason to retreat.

We'll trade.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1Bp5/3p4/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
Some players may try to get aggressive with their central pawns. 

But recall that after castling, our rook can come into the game.

This check is hard to deal with. 

There are many tactics having to do with Ne4 and Ne5 depending on what Black plays.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n5/1Bpp4/8/2N2N2/PPPP1P.text:
The knight blocks.

And we'll castle.

r1bqkbnr/pppn1ppp/4p3/8/4N3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
...Nd7 is necessary before ...Ngf6 to support the knight.

We'll advance in the center anyway.

r2qk2r/pp1bbppp/2n2n2/1BppN3/3P4/2N5/PPP.text:
When Black defends...

We can take the bishop on d7.

r2qkb1r/pbp2p1p/1pn1pp2/8/3P4/4BN2/PPPQ1.text:
And we'll castle queenside.

We'll continue with moves like Bc4 and Kb1. 

Rhe1 is also on the horizon. 

Our strategy consists of superior central control and keeping a better pawn structure.

r3k2r/pp1qbppp/2n2n2/1BPp4/8/2N5/PPP2PPP.text:
And now we make Black's position really awkward, since ...Bxc5 allows Re1+.

Black will most likely castle. 

So we can continue with moves like Be3-Bd4, and even b4 to hang on to the pawn.

rn1qk1nr/pp1bbppp/8/1BpN4/8/5N2/PPPPQPPP.text:
And we're a pawn up. 

If ...Bxb5, Qxb5+ and Black is in more trouble: ...Nc6 and the b7-pawn falls. 

It's now time to consolidate. 

So if Black just develops with ...Nc6, b3 for Bb2 and O-O are good options for White.

rn1qkbnr/pp1b1ppp/8/1Bpp4/8/2N2N2/PPPP1P.text:
Blocking with the bishop is a blunder. 

Many people fall for this. You'll notice that the bishop on d7 disconnects the queen's defense of d4.

We'll give a check on e2, defending the bishop first.

rnb1k2r/pp3pp1/3bpq1p/2p5/3P4/3B1N2/PPP1.text:
If you see Black play ...c5 at this point, you can just capture.

This forces Black's bishop to move once again and Black hasn't achieved much.

rnb1k2r/pp3pp1/4pq1p/2b5/8/3B1N2/PPP1QPP.text:
We can continue with sound, developing moves like Re1, c3 and Be3. 

Sure, Black has removed our central pawn, but we'll get a lot of activity in exchange for that.

We'll centralize both rooks, bringing them to the open and semi-open d- and e-files, and enjoy more space for our pieces.

rnb1k2r/ppp2pp1/3bpq1p/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
Black develops as well.

And White is better after Qe2.

We have stronger central control and more active pieces.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3bpq2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
If Black just develops their dark-squared bishop...

We won't play Bg5 right away. 

Rather, we'll set up a trap.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2pp1/4pq1p/8/3P4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
That's why ...h6 is the most popular move. 

We can simply continue developing at this point.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/4pq2/8/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
And once the queen recaptures...

We threaten Bg5, attacking the queen.

rnb2rk1/ppp2pp1/3bpq1p/8/3P4/3B1N2/PPP1Q.text: For example, castling, believe it or not, is a very popular blunder here.

rnb2rk1/ppp2pp1/3bpq1p/8/3PQ3/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
We have Qe4, threatening checkmate!

And now Black must lose a pawn to prevent checkmate or simply acquire a worse position. 

If ...Qf5, we have Qh4 with a discovered attack and Bxh6 sacrifices in the air!

rnb2rk1/ppp2ppp/3bpq2/6B1/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
The queen is trapped.

Good game!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/4pp2/8/8/5N2/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Some players like recapturing with the g-pawn because the doubled pawns are actually not weak. 

They can control many squares in the center, and the rook also gains a semi-open g-file.

We'll play d4, controlling the center and opening up our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/4N3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
This is the most popular move at this point.

But it's not the most accurate.

We will take.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/4P3/2N2N2/PPPP1.text:
3...c5, gaining space, is also played 10% of the time, but it's just bad. 

Black is simply too far down in development and is focusing on pawn play more than they should be.

We'll capture on d5 first.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/8/2N2N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black recaptures, and you'll notice the pawns are potential targets. 

So we'll develop quickly first. 

The check on b5 brings the bishop out and attacks the king. 

We're clearing the way for castling.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black plays ...d5.

And we activate both knights in response.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/8/4p3/2N2N2/PPPP1PP.text:
Black makes the trade on e4 over 30% of the time, making it the most popular move.

Black wants to get rid of our central pawn and target our knights in the center.

We'll recapture.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black prepares the French.

We get our kingside knight out.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the second and last study of the Two Knights French! 

Black could also play the very natural capture on e4 on move 3. 

Besides, they could just expand on the queenside with 3...c5. 

Let's learn some ways to deal with these options!

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p5/3pPb1p/3P3P/8/PPP2P.text:
Black responds with ...h5 43% of the time, freeing up the h7-square and preventing our h-pawn from advancing any further.

This is a direct way of preventing us from trapping their bishop.

We'll develop our dark-squared bishop to g5 in order to pin Black's e-pawn, since they want to play ...e6 now.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3pPb2/3P4/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Black develops the bishop to f5 65% of the time, which is one of the two main moves.

The idea behind this move is to develop the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before Black plays ...e6.

I'm going to recommend h4, which in my opinion is the most critical and challenging way to fight Black's setup.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/3pP2P/3P2P1/5P2/.text:
We trap Black's bishop with h5 and Black has no way to save it!

This is one of the ideas behind h4.

Black must not play ...e6.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p1b1/3pP3/3P2PP/5P2/P.text: Black retreats the bishop to g6.

Black moves the bishop to e4.

rn1qkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3pPb2/3P3P/8/PPP2P.text:
The move ...e6 is simply a blunder, and it's played almost 20% of the time!

rn2kbnr/4ppp1/2p1P3/1p1p2Bp/p2P3P/1Q6/P1.text: Black pushes the a-pawn forward and attacks our queen.

rn2kbnr/4ppp1/2p1P3/pp1p2Bp/3P3P/1Q6/P1P.text:
Black continues expanding on the queenside.

Once they capture our rook and their queen is stuck, this is the standard approach.

We simply castle our king.

rn2kbnr/p3p1p1/1pp1p3/3p2Bp/3P3P/1Q6/P1P.text: Black captures the pawn on e6.

Now once we move the knight from b1, Black won't be able to save the queen.

rn2kbnr/p3ppp1/1pp1P3/3p2Bp/3P3P/1Q6/P1P.text:
Black goes for ...b6 to defend.

We'll castle next move.

rn2kbnr/p3ppp1/2p1P3/1p1p2Bp/3P3P/1Q6/P1.text:
Black defends against Qxb7 by pushing the b-pawn.

rn2kbnr/pQ2ppp1/2p1P3/3p2Bp/3q3P/8/P1P2P.text:
We capture the pawn on b7.

Not only does this win Black's rook, but it also threatens a checkmate with Qc8#. 

Those threats, in conjunction with the useful retreating move Be3, secure White a winning advantage!

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp5/3pP1Bp/3P3P/3b4/PPP.text:
Most often, Black opts to exchange the light-squared bishops on d3.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/1qp5/3pPbBp/3P3P/8/PPP2P.text:

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/2p1P3/3p1BBp/3P3P/8/P1P2.text:
But we push e6 with an advantage!

We are down an exchange, but Black is really cramped and underdeveloped.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/2p1P3/3p1BBp/7P/5N2/P1P2.text:
We get a similar position to the 6...Qxb2 variation.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/2p1P3/3p2Bp/3P3P/3Q4/P1P.text:
Black captures the rook and threatens our knight and the a2-pawn.

This move defends the knight and pawn, but it also takes away some squares from Black's queen and attacks the b7-pawn.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/2p1P3/3p2Bp/3q3P/1Q6/P1P.text:
Black captures the pawn on d4.

This is another option.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/2p5/3pP1Bp/3P3P/3Q4/PqP2.text:
Black will probably capture on b2 at some point.

Black moves the queen over to g4 and defends the bishop.

rn2kbnr/pp2ppp1/2p5/3pPbBp/7P/3B1N2/PqP2.text:
Black could opt to take on b2.

rn1qkbnr/pp1bppp1/2p4p/3pP3/3P2PP/8/PPP2.text:
Black retreats the bishop to d7.

rn1qkbnr/pp2p1p1/2p1p2p/3p4/3P2PP/3Q1P2/.text:

rn1qkbnr/pp2p1p1/2p1p2p/3p4/3P2PP/3b1P2/.text: Black obliges and trades on d3.

Black accepts the sacrifice by capturing the pawn on e6.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p4p/3pP3/3Pb1PP/8/PPP2.text:
Sometimes Black moves the bishop to e4 in order to induce f3 before going back to h7.

rn1qkbnr/pp2ppp1/2p4p/3pPb2/3P3P/8/PPP2P.text:
Black responds with ...h6, freeing up the h7-square for their bishop.

This move occurs just over 30% of the time.

We'll use the opportunity to continue with g4.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppb/2p4p/3pP3/3P2PP/5P2/PPP.text:
Black retreats the bishop to the only safe square, h7.

And here we implement an important positional sacrifice: e6.

We want to disrupt Black's coordination and pawn structure as much as possible and slow down their development.

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppb/2p4p/3pP3/3P2PP/8/PPP2P.text:

rn2k1nr/p1qb1pp1/2p1p2p/2PpP3/1P4PP/P1p1.text: Black retreats the queen to c7 and attacks the e5-pawn.

rn2k1nr/p1qb1ppp/2p1p3/2PpP3/1P1Q2PP/P1p.text:
We'll continue with Qd4, looking to capture the pawn on c3 at some point.

rn2k1nr/p1qb1ppp/2p1p3/2PpP3/1P4PP/P1p5/.text: Black retreats the queen to c7 and attacks the e5-pawn.

Black prevents b4.

rn2k1nr/p2b1pp1/2p1p2p/q1PpP3/6PP/P1p1B3.text:

Black pushes their b-pawn forward and prevents b4.

Black captures the pawn on c3, but we were prepared for this.

Our knight is pretty annoying on c5, so Black trades the bishop for it.

rn2kbnr/p2b1pp1/2p1p2p/qp1pP3/N2P2PP/2P1.text:
Black attacks the knight with ...b5.

rn2kbnr/p2b1ppp/2p1p3/qp1pP3/N2P2PP/2P5/.text:
Black goes for ...b5 instead, attacking the knight once again.

The queen comes out to b6, attacking the b2-pawn.

rn2kbnr/pp1b1pp1/2p1p2p/q2pP3/N2P2PP/4B3.text:
Black moves the queen out to a5 and attacks our king and knight.

Black opens up the dark-squared bishop, "kills" the light-squared bishop, and sets up a solid light-squared pawn chain with ...e6.

rn2kbnr/pp1b1ppp/2p1p3/q2pP3/N2P2PP/8/PP.text:
Black moves the queen out to a5 and gives a check.

rn2kbnr/pp1bpppp/1qp5/3pP3/3P2PP/8/PPP2P.text:
Black retreats the bishop to d7.

rn2kbnr/pp2p1p1/2pqp2p/3p4/3P1PPP/3Q4/PP.text:
We'll implement the f4-idea, looking to play Nf3.

Black declines the sacrifice and attacks the pawn with their queen.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppb/2pqP2p/3p4/3P2PP/8/PPP2P.text:
Black declines the sacrifice and attacks the pawn with their queen.

We'll take on f7.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppp/1qp5/3pPb2/3P3P/8/PPP2PP.text:
Black moves the queen to b6 only  1% of the time.

The idea is that Black is preventing us from easily developing the dark-squared bishop.

If Black hasn't stopped us from doing so, we'll attack the bishop with g4.

rn3b1r/pp2pkpb/2pq1n1p/3p4/3P1PPP/8/PPP5.text:
Black develops the kingside knight to f6 and attacks the g4-pawn, which is now weaker.

It seems like we can't play Nf3 now because of the threat on g4, but that is exactly what we'll do!

The knight on f3 will give us many crucial prospects in the position, combined with the next move we'll play.

rn3b1r/pp2pkpb/2pq3p/3p3P/3P1Pn1/5N2/PPP.text:
We push our h-pawn to h5, further cramping Black's position. 

With the space advantage and great attacking prospects on the kingside, White has sufficient compensation for the pawn.

We'll look to continue with Bh3 and Ne5. Black's pieces are all over the place.

rn3b1r/pp2pkpb/2pq3p/3p4/3P1PnP/5N2/PPP5.text: Black grabs the pawn on g4.

rn3bnr/pp2pkpb/2pq3p/3p2P1/3P3P/8/PPP2P2.text:
We push our g-pawn to g5. 

White now has a convincing edge.

Black's king is exposed and our attacking possibilites are tremendous.

We can continue with Nf3 and Bh3.

rn3bnr/pp2pkpb/2pq3p/3p4/3P2PP/5P2/PPP5/.text:
Black recaptures on f7.

We' ll push the pawn to f4, gaining some space and looking to develop our knight behind it.

This takes even more control of the e5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...c6.

We'll defend the pawn with Be2.

Black develops the knight to e7, preparing ...O-O and looking to jump the knight to d5 or f5.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2b1P3/3p1P2/P2Bn3/1.text: Black jumps the knight into e3 and attacks our queen, trying to disrupt our plans.

But we can simply move the queen to f3.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2b1Pn2/3p1P2/P7/1PP.text:
Black jumps their knight into f5, aiming for the e3-square.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2bnP3/3p1P2/P7/1PPN.text:
Black jumps their knight to d5 and attacks the f4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n4n/2PpP3/5P2/8/PPP3PP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight out to h6, supporting the g4-square and looking to jump the knight to f5 in the future.

r1bqkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2PpP3/8/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black opts for ...Nc6 in this study, attacking our e5-pawn. Expect to see this more than 65% of the time.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2P1P3/3p1P2/4B3/PP.text:
Things might seem dangerous if Black pushes the d-pawn to d4, attacking our bishop and interfering with the defense of the c5-pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpP3/5P2/8/PPP3PP.text:
Most often does Black try to go after our c5-pawn.

Black exchanges bishops on e2.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n4n/2PpP3/5Pb1/2P5/PP4P.text:
Black uses the control of the g4-square and activates the bishop with tempo on our queen.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p2n/2PpP3/5P2/2P5/PP2Q.text:
Finally, Black opens up the dark-squared bishop and attacks our c5-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPn2/5P2/2P1B3/PP.text: Black jumps the knight into f5 and threatens our dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPn2/5P2/2P5/PP2Q.text:
We slide the bishop back to f2.

r2qkbnr/pp2pppp/2n5/2PpPb2/5P2/8/PPP3PP/.text:

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPb2/5P2/4BN2/PPP.text:
We'll defend with the bishop and claim an advantage.

r2qkbnr/pp3ppp/2n1p3/2PpPb2/5P2/5N2/PPP3.text: Black opens up an attack on the c5-pawn.

Black strikes in the center with ...c5 just over 20% of the time, challenging our d4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this chapter, we're going to conclude our analysis of the Advance Caro-Kann by learning how to play against Black's 3...c5.

r1bq1r2/pp2n1p1/1b2p1k1/nP1pPpN1/6Q1/P7/.text: Black pushes ...f5 and attacks our queen, which is to be expected.

r1bq1r2/pp2n1p1/1b2pPk1/nP1p2N1/6Q1/P7/1.text:
We capture en passant.

Black jumps the knight into d5.

We'll play the standard h3 idea.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/8/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
The most common reply is 3...d6, which is played more than 40% of the time.

Black opens up the bishop and prepares to fight against our center in hypermodern fashion.

We'll develop our bishop to c4, and our idea is to play Qe2, castle, and wait for the right moment to go e5.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3pp1p1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black decides to restrict our bishop with ...e6 12% of the time.

However, this approach is passive and leaves their own bishop stuck on c8.

We'll castle for now.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black fianchettoes the bishop.

We'll develop the kingside knight. 

There are various pawn pushes Black can now implement, such as ...c6, ...c5 or ...d6.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2pp1np1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP1.text:
Black continues with ...c6, looking to support a future expansion in the center and on the queenside.

This gives us time to push our e-pawn forward and attack Black's knight!

The move 6...dxe5 would now transpose to the main line.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2pp2p1/3nP3/2BP4/5N2/PPP.text:
Black jumps the knight into d5.

It's important to prevent the bishop from coming to g4, so we'll play h3 for now.

rnbqk2r/ppp1npbp/3pp1p1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black develops the knight to e7.

We'll continue improving and bring the rook to the e-file this time.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks the e4-pawn 45% of the time.

We defend the e-pawn and support a future e5 by moving our queen to e2.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/3ppnp1/8/2BPP3/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
Black continues with ...e6, negating the effect of the c4-bishop and looking to support a future central expansion.

We can push e5, though, before Black gets any chance to expand.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/4p1p1/3nP3/2B5/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
Black escapes to the center.

Since the knight has left its post, there is some weakness on the dark squares.

We can look to take advantage of this by bringing our bishop to g5 and pressuring Black's queen.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/4pnp1/4p3/2BP4/5N2/PPP1Q.text:
Black captures the pawn on e5.

We'll recapture with the pawn and keep the pressure on the knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
The Modern Defense is similar to the Pirc in the sense of fianchettoing the bishop.

Expect to see it only 3% of the time, but it occured in more than 125 million games.

By choosing this move order, Black is flexible with their pawn pushes and doesn't always have to commit to ...d6.

We'll play d4 anyway.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this chapter, we will be taking a look at the move 1...g6, which signifes the Modern Defense.

We'll explain the ideas behind it and learn how to fight against it.

Let's go.

rnbqnrk1/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2p1P3/2BP4/5N1P/P.text:
Black tries to undermine our structure by striking in the center with ...c5.

Not much merit to letting Black trade off many pawns in the center, so we'll capture instead.

rnbqnrk1/pp2ppbp/6p1/2P1p3/2B5/5N1P/PPP1.text:
Black captures the e5-pawn, which they deem more useful than the c5-pawn.

That's okay. We'll just castle.

We shouldn't rush with recapturing on e5, as it could become dangerous if our king is not safe.

rnbqnrk1/ppp1ppbp/3p2p1/4P3/2BP4/5N2/PPP.text:
Black retreats the knight to e8.

We've pushed the knight back.

Let's restrict the light-squared bishop further with h3 now.

r1b1k2r/pp2ppbp/n5p1/1Np1P3/5Bn1/2P2N2/P.text:
We finally support the e5-pawn by developing the dark-squared bishop. 

Black's pieces are all over the place and waiting to be attacked, while we have harmony in the position.

White has a borderline winning advantage and should continue with h3, Be2 and O-O.

r1b1k2r/pp2ppbp/n5p1/1Np1P3/6n1/2P2N2/PP.text: Black covers the c7-square, but their knight is passive.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2p2pp1/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP.text:
Black develops the queenside knight.

We'll improve our rook.

Both sides developing calmly and in a traditional manner.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP2.text:
We'll move our rook to the e-file. 

White now has a pleasant position and can look to continue with c3 and Bf4, strengthening the presence on the dark squares.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/1np2pp1/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP2.text: Black jumps the knight into b6 and attacks the c4-bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/1np2pp1/8/3P4/1B3N1P/PPP.text:
But we can simply slide the bishop back to b3. 

White now has a pleasant edge, and can look to continue with a4 and Bf4.

r1bqk1nr/pp1nppbp/2p3p1/8/3PN3/5N1P/PPP2.text:
Black develops the queenside knight.

We'll prepare kingside castling by developing the bishop to the most active square.

r1bqk2r/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/8/2BPN3/5N1P/PPP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight.

It's more efficient to capture than to defend our knight or retreat.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP2P.text:
Black recaptures with the d7-knight.

We'll castle.

rn2k2r/pp2p1bp/4p1p1/8/4p3/2P1B2P/PP3PP1.text:
We'll develop our bishop to e3 and White is simply better.

Black's tripled and isolated pawns on the e-file yield more than enough compensation for the pawn that we are down.

We can look to continue by long castling.

rn2k2r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2P1bb2/4N3/3B3P/PPP2P.text:
We support our knight with Bd3. 

White is now simply up a pawn and can continue with c3 and Kc2.

Black's ...c5 attempt hasn't proven worthy at all.

rn2k2r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2P1bb2/4N3/7P/PPP2PP1.text: Black develops the light-squared bishop with tempo.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/4b1p1/4q1N1/2Q1p3/2P4P/PP.text:
Black deals with both threats by moving the bishop to e6.

We'll trade.

rn2k2r/pp2ppbp/4q1p1/8/2Q1p3/2P4P/PP3PP1.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

We trade queens on e6, forcing Black to recapture and triple their e-pawns!

This whole line is pretty much forced.

rnb1k1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2q5/4P3/2P2N2/PP3P.text:
Black captures the pawn on c5.

We'll play the creative Na3, aiming for Nb5 and Be3. 

This move is the antidote for Black's approach.

rnb1k1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/q1P5/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
The idea is to get the queen out to a5 and fork our king and the pawn.

We'll block with c3.

rnb1k1nr/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/q3b3/8/N1P1BN2/PP.text:
Black captures the pawn with their bishop.

We'll take.

rnb1k1nr/pp2pp1p/6p1/q3p3/2B5/N1P1B3/PP3.text:
We are down a pawn, but the piece activity and the lead in development more than compensate for it.

We can continue with Qb3 and castle.

Meanwhile, Black has only got their queen developed, and their e5-pawn is a liability more than it is an asset.

rnb1k1nr/pp2pp1p/6p1/q3p3/8/N1P1B3/PP3PP.text:
Black recaptures with the d-pawn.

Otherwise there would have been Bd4 problems.

rnb1k1nr/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2q5/4P3/N1P2N2/PP.text:
Black opens up their light-squared bishop with ...d6.

We develop our bishop to e3 and attack Black's queen!

If Black now retreats the queen to c7, we can continue with Nb5.

rnb1k1nr/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/q7/4P3/N1P1BN2/PP.text:
Black moves the queen to a5, allowing an interesting idea.

We can sacrifice the pawn on e5!

We want to either trade off Black's bishop or make them block it.

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/2q5/4P3/N1P2N2/PP3.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and threatens the e4-pawn.

It's most logical to push the pawn to e5.

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/2q1P3/6n1/N1P2N2/PP.text:
Black jumps to g4.

It seems like we can't save the e5-pawn, since it's attacked with three pieces.

But we counted on this and we have Qd4, offering a trade!

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/4P3/3P2n1/N4N2/PP3P.text:
We recapture with the c-pawn and now our center is back together. 

White now has a considerable edge. 

We want to play Nb5 and h3 to force the knight back. 

From there, we will target Black's weaknesses.

rnb1k2r/pp1pppbp/6p1/4P3/3q2n1/N1P2N2/PP.text: Black trades the queens on d4.

rnb1k2r/pp2pp1p/6p1/2P1b1N1/4p3/7P/PPP2P.text:
Black captures the e5-pawn.

And we see a trade of pawns in the center.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2q1P3/3Q2n1/N1P2N2.text:
Black opens up the c8-bishop and supports the queen with ...d6.

We'll trade the queens.

We have a plan B.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2P1P1N1/4p3/7P/PPP2P.text:
Black trades the queens on d1.

We'll recapture.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p1P3/6n1/N1P2N2/PP3.text:
Black recaptures on c5.

Instead of defending the e5-pawn, we can jump our knight to b5 and threaten the devastating Nc7.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2q1P1N1/4p3/2P4P/PP3.text:
Black captures the pawn on c5.

The e5-pawn is vulnerable.

However, if Black didn't want to trade queens on d1, let's see if they want to do it on d4.

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/4q1N1/3Qp3/2P4P/PP3P.text:
Nope. Black captures on e5.

But we didn't just place our queen on d4 so that we trade.

We'll slide to c4 now and attack both the bishop and the f7-pawn.

If Black now castles their king, we have a nice tactic with Nxf7!

rnb1k2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/q1P1P1N1/4p3/7P/PPP2.text:
Looking to immediately regain the pawn, Black moves the queen out to a5 and gives a check to our king.

This leads to a fun line where we eventually provoke Black to triple their pawns on the e-file!

We'll block the check with c3, for starters.

rnbq1rk1/pp2pp1p/2p2bp1/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP2.text:
Black castles, which allows for a positional idea by us.

We move our bishop out to h6 and attack Black's rook, since Black has left a hole on g7.

If Black now defends with ...Bg7, we should respond with Qd2 and O-O.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2p2pp1/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP2P.text:
Black castles their king.

We'll do the same.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2p3p1/8/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black continues with ...c6, preparing a central expansion with ...d5, just under 5% of the time.

This reminds of the Caro-Kann, except the dark-squared bishop is already on g7.

We'll get both knights out.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p5/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black plays ...c5, trying to activate the g7-bishop, 7% of the time.

This isn't particularly good at all.

We can actually call Black's bluff and capture on c5.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/3p4/3PP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black goes for ...d5.

They would love to activate their light-squared bishop next, which is why we will play h3.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/8/3Pp3/2N2N1P/PPP.text:
Black captures the pawn on e4.

We'll recapture.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black fianchettoes the bishop.

We'll develop the kingside knight.

rnbqk2r/pp2pp1p/2p2bp1/8/3P4/5N1P/PPP2PP.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

Let's finish kingside development.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/3PP3/2N2N1P/P.text:
If Black activates the knight before capturing on e4, we shouldn't waste any time.

Let's push e5.

If Black now retreats the knight, we can continue with Be3 and Qd2.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/8/3PN3/5N1P/PPP2P.text:
Most often, Black develops the kingside knight to f6.

We'll take.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/3pP3/3Pn3/2N2N1P/P.text:
Black jumps the knight into e4 instead.

We'll trade.

There's no reason to leave Black's knight in the center.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p3p1/4P3/3Pp3/5N1P/PPP2.text:
Black recaptures on e4.

We'll attack the weak e4-pawn by jumping our knight to g5.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/6p1/2p1P1N1/3Pp3/7P/PPP2.text:
Black pushes the c-pawn and counterattacks our center.

A move like c3 is definitely playable here, but I recommend we capture on c5.

It's a more direct approach that asks Black whether they want to trade queens.

rnbqk2r/pp3pbp/2p2pp1/8/3P4/5N1P/PPP2PP1.text:
Black recaptures with the e-pawn.

This doubles their pawns but keeps their kingside safer.

We'll bring our bishop to c4 next.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black is intending to fianchetto their bishop.

We'll expand in the center with d4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text: In this study, we'll conclude our analysis of The Modern Defense by learning how to respond if Black moves their c-pawn on move three.

rnbqr1k1/pp2pp1p/2p2bpB/8/2BP4/5N1P/PPP2.text:
We castle our king.

We should look to consolidate and improve with c3, Re1 and Qd2.

We have a lead in activity and there is no real coordination between Black's pieces.
Black moves the rook to e8 instead.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3q4/8/2PB1Q2/P1P2PP.text: Black captures on d5 with the queen.

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3q4/8/2PB2Q1/P1P2PP.text:
And we slide our queen over to g3 and attack two of Black's pawns.

The bishop pair, in conjunction with the superior piece activity, should secure White a pleasant game.

Even though we've got doubled c-pawns and are down a pawn, we have a lot of compensation.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/1bP1pn2/4N3/8/3B4/PPP2PP.text:
And we jump our knight to e5. 

White now has a comfortable advantage and can continue with Re1, Bg5 and Qf3.

The idea is to put pressure on the f6-knight and the kingside overall since we are ahead in development and activity.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/1bP1pn2/8/8/3B1N2/PPP2PP.text: Black retreats the bishop to b6 to avoid the trade.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3n4/2PP4/3B1N2/P2Q.text:
We take some space and attack Black's knight once more with c4!

Down a pawn, but our piece activity and lead in development more than compensate for it. 

Black has lost a lot of tempi as well.

We'll look to continue with Bb2, Rad1 and Rfe1.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3n4/3P4/2bB1N2/PPP.text:
Black captures on d5 with the knight.

We'll take the bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3n4/3P4/3B1N2/P1PQ.text: Black moves the knight back to d5.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/8/3P4/2nB1N2/P1P2P.text:
Black recaptures on c3, attacking our queen.

The d2-square is natural to attack the knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3P4/3b4/3B1N2/PPP.text:
Black captures on d4 with the bishop.

In that case, we'll take the knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/1b1PP3/2NB1N2.text:
Black develops the dark-squared bishop and pins our c3-knight.

We'll simply castle.

We have a plan if Black goes after our knight.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3PP3/2bB1N2/P.text:
Black does capture.

We have to throw in exd5, because we lose the e4-pawn otherwise.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3P4/3n4/2bB1N2/PPP2.text:
Black captures on d4 with the knight.

We'll recapture on c3, naturally.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3P4/8/2PB1n2/P1P2PP.text:
Black captures the knight on f3.

We'll recapture with the queen.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3PP3/2N2N2/P.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and adds an attacker to the e4-pawn.

We defend the e-pawn by developing our light-squared bishop to d3.

If Black now goes for ...Nb4, we should continue with e5 and, ideally, Bg5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2np4/8/3PP3/2N5/PPP2PP.text:
We expand in the center with d4. 

Of course, White has an objective edge, and can look to set up with Nge2, h3 and g4, taking a note from Chapter 5.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2np4/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1PP.text: Black continues with ...d6, opening up the light-squared bishop.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n1p3/3p4/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black follows up on their previous move by advancing the d-pawn and challenging our central pawn.

We'll expand in the center with d4, as we don't want to trade and open up Black's pieces.

Our general plan is now Be3 and castling.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n1p3/8/4P3/2N5/PPPP1P.text:
Black continues with ...e6, supporting a future advance with ...d5.

We'll develop our kingside knight to f3.

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/2n5/8/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black replies with 1...Nc6, which is only played 1% of the time.

With this move, Black hopes that you will play d4, get met with ...d5, and an immediate fight in the center.

I recommend we proceed with 2. Nc3. The move ...e5 now transposes to the Vienna.

rn1qk2r/pb1nbppp/1p2p3/2ppP1N1/3P1P2/2PB.text:
But we placed the knight on g5 to keep it there, so we will protect it with f4.

White now simply has a pleasant position with promising attacking prospects in the middlegame.

We'll look to continue with Be3 and O-O. Black might have a hard time castling.

rn1qk2r/pb1nbppp/1p2p3/2ppP1N1/3P4/2PB4/.text: They attack our knight with the bishop instead.

rn1qkb1r/pb1n1ppp/1p2p3/2ppP3/3P4/2PB1N2.text:
Black moves the knight back to d7.

I suggest we jump forward here.

Black shouldn't play ...h6 because we can sacrifice on e6 and expose their weakened light squares.

rn1qkb1r/pb1p1ppp/1p2pn2/2p5/3PP3/2PB1N2.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks the e4-pawn.

We can protect the pawn with the queen. This is better than pushing e5, since we would just be giving the d5-square to Black.

And we aren't looking to push c4 anymore once we've played c3.

rn1qkb1r/pb3ppp/1p2pn2/2pp4/3PP3/2PB1N2/.text:
However, once Black expands with ...d5, that square is taken by the pawn.

So we will push e5 now!

This closes the center with tempo and opens up our light-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/3nP3/3P4/3B1N2/P.text:
Black jumps the knight into d5.

This is where we see why leaving room for the c-pawn is important.

We take some space and attack Black's knight once more with c4!

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/4P3/1nPP4/3B1N2/.text: Black jumps the knight into b4 and threatens to capture our bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/4P3/1nPP4/5N2/PP.text:
But we simply slide back to e2.

White should look to continue with a3, Nc3 and O-O.

Black might have a hard time fighting against our active central pawn structure.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2pn2/8/3PP3/3B1N2/PP.text:
Black develops the kingside knight and attacks the e4-pawn.

We'll push to e5 and counterattack.

I prefer this aggressive option to defending the pawn.

rn1qkbnr/p1p2ppp/1p2p3/3b4/3P4/3B1N2/PPP.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

We'll attack it with c4.

rn1qkbnr/pb1p1ppp/1p2p3/2p5/3PP3/3B1N2/P.text:
Black immediately strikes with ...c5.

Now it's logical to connect the pawns with c3.

rn1qkbnr/pbp2ppp/1p2p3/3p4/3PP3/3B1N2/PP.text:
Black quickly expands with ...d5.

Both e5 and capturing the pawn are playable, but I recommend taking so that we can win an additional tempo.

Black will rarely ever recapture with the pawn because that condemns the bishop on b7 to death.

rn1qkbnr/pbp2ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/2NB1N2/PP3.text:
And we develop our queenside knight. 

The position is quite pleasant and we have relatively simple development with Qe2, Bf4 and castling.

We want to take even more control of the e5-square and of the e-file in general, utilizing our space advantage.

rn1qkbnr/pbp2ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/3B1N2/PP3P.text: Black retreats the queen to d8 instead.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/3PP3/3B4/PPP2P.text:
Black continues with ...e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop and preparing to fight against our center.

We'll develop the kingside knight to f3 for now.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black fianchettoes the bishop and attacks the e4-pawn.

I recommend defending with the bishop here instead of committing with Nc3.

We should leave our options open for the c-pawn to move.

rn2kbnr/pbp2ppp/1p2p3/3q4/3P4/3B1N2/PPP2.text:
Black recaptures with the queen.

We expand in the center and attack Black's queen with c4.

If Black now moves the queen to h5, we should defend with Be2 and then proceed with Nc3 and O-O.

rnbqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/1n2p3/p3P3/P1P5/6R1/1P.text:
We move our rook over to g3! 

Our flexible rook is now an additional annoying piece on the kingside, and hard to attack.

The arising position is roughly equal, but White has strong attacking chances.

The move ...d5 should now be met with cxd5.

rnbqkb1r/1ppp1ppp/1n2p3/p3P3/P1P5/R7/1P1.text: Black pushes ...e6 and opens up an attack on our rook.

rnbqkb1r/1ppppppp/1n6/p3P3/P1P5/8/1P1P1P.text:
Black stops a5 directly, but allows for an extremely useful idea.

We lift our rook up to a3! 

Inspired by Jeroen Bosch's article in SOS/New in Chess, I'm sharing this idea with you.
